items.prompt: Which truth pattern is valid for a first-true binary search over increasing candidates?

options.text: false, true, false, true.
false, false, ..., false, true, true, ..., true.
true, false, true.
Any pattern, because indices are ordered.

feedback.reason: A first-true search requires one false-to-true transition.

blocks.text: One transition makes each side eliminable

Let b be the first candidate with P(b) = true. False-to-true monotonicity means every candidate before b is false and every candidate from b onward is true; either region may be empty at a domain endpoint.

items: If P(mid) is true, b <= mid, so candidates after mid are irrelevant and mid must remain possible.
If P(mid) is false, b > mid, so mid and every earlier candidate can be removed.
Alternation or a return to false would invalidate one of these whole-side deductions.

blocks.title: Formal direction
blocks.text: For all a <= b, P(a) = true must imply P(b) = true. Equivalently, P(b) = false implies every earlier P(a) is false.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.alternating: Alternation creates several false-to-true and true-to-false transitions, so neither midpoint result can classify an entire ordered side.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.true_false_true: Truth cannot return after becoming false in a single-boundary search.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary: Ordered indices do not make an arbitrary predicate monotonic.

items.prompt: Which truth pattern supports a last-true search?

options.text: false values followed by true values.
true, false, true, false.
true, true, ..., true, false, false, ..., false.
Exactly one true value anywhere in the domain.

feedback.reason: A last-true boundary separates a true prefix from a false suffix.

blocks.text: Last true uses the opposite transition
Let b be the final candidate with P(b) = true. In a true-to-false pattern, every candidate through b is true and every later candidate is false.

items: P(mid) = true proves b >= mid; retain mid and search larger candidates.
P(mid) = false proves b < mid; discard mid and every later candidate.
An isolated true value with unknown location lacks these implications and is not an ordinary boundary-search contract.

blocks.title: Mirror relationship
blocks.text: First true searches a false prefix followed by a true suffix. Last true searches a true prefix followed by a false suffix.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_then_true: That pattern supports first true rather than last true under the same direction.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.alternating: After a true midpoint, a later false and still later true can exist, so searching only one side may discard the final true.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.single_true_only_anywhere: Its location cannot be found by ordinary boundary search without additional structure.

items.prompt: The predicate feasible(x) means a machine with capacity x can finish all jobs. More capacity can never hurt. Which boundary is natural when minimizing capacity?

options.text: The last true x.
The first false x.
Any feasible x.
The first x for which feasible(x) is true.

feedback.reason: The feasibility pattern is false for insufficient capacity and true from the minimum sufficient capacity onward.

blocks.text: More capacity preserves feasibility
If capacity x can complete all jobs, any y >= x can run the same schedule with at least as much available capacity. Thus feasible(x) implies feasible(y), establishing false-to-true monotonicity.

items: Capacities below the requirement form an infeasible prefix.
The minimum sufficient capacity is the first true point.
Larger feasible capacities satisfy the constraints but fail the minimization objective.

blocks.title: Reuse-the-witness proof
blocks.text: A common monotonicity proof reuses the construction that made x feasible and shows the relaxed candidate y cannot invalidate it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_true: Larger values may remain true indefinitely, so the last true may simply be the domain maximum.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_false: The first false capacity is infeasible and lies in the prefix before the requested first feasible boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_true: Any feasible value may be larger than the minimum.

items.prompt: The predicate valid(d) means all items can be placed with minimum separation at least d. Increasing d can only make placement harder. Which boundary is natural when maximizing separation?

options.text: The first true d.
The last d for which valid(d) remains true.
The final false d.
Any false d.

feedback.reason: The truth pattern is a true prefix followed by a false suffix.

blocks.text: Larger required separation only removes placements

If all items can be placed with separation d, the same placement also satisfies every smaller separation. Conversely, failure at d means every larger minimum separation is at least as restrictive and also fails.

items: Small distances form a valid prefix.
After one transition, larger distances form an invalid suffix.
Maximization therefore returns the last true distance immediately before that suffix.

blocks.title: Constraint-direction rule
blocks.text: When increasing a candidate tightens a requirement, feasibility often changes true-to-false. When increasing it adds resources, feasibility often changes false-to-true.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_true: Small values may already be feasible and do not maximize separation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_false: A false candidate violates the placement constraint, and the final false point is unrelated to the last valid distance before the transition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_false: One invalid distance only proves that it and larger distances fail; it does not identify the greatest smaller distance that remains valid.

items.prompt: A predicate over integers is true exactly when x is even. Is it suitable for ordinary first-true binary search over 0 through n?

options.text: Yes. Every numeric predicate is monotonic.
Yes, because 0 may be the first true value.
No. Truth alternates and does not form one false-to-true boundary.
Yes, if an upper-biased midpoint is used.

feedback.reason: Parity changes truth repeatedly across the domain.

blocks.text: Write the predicate values in candidate order
For x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, the predicate “x is even” yields true, false, true, false, true. Truth reverses at every adjacent candidate rather than persisting as a suffix.

items: If an odd midpoint is false, a larger even candidate may still be true.
If an even midpoint is true, a later odd candidate becomes false.
Neither result classifies a whole side, so ordinary first-true elimination is unsupported.

blocks.title: A true first element is insufficient
blocks.text: Knowing that 0 is true answers this particular first-true query directly, but it does not make parity a monotonic predicate or justify binary-search updates on a general subdomain.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_numeric: Numeric order supplies before and after, but parity truth still alternates instead of persisting on one ordered side.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_first_zero: Although 0 is true, candidate 1 is false and candidate 2 becomes true again, so the predicate itself has multiple transitions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_mid: Upper bias can guarantee boundary progress, but it cannot make a false odd midpoint classify all larger candidates when larger evens are true.

items.prompt: For n >= 1, what should a first-true search return when the predicate is false for every candidate in a [0, n) domain?

options.text: The last midpoint examined.
n, the boundary after the final candidate.

feedback.reason: A half-open search can represent the absence of a true candidate with the exclusive upper boundary.

blocks.text: No true suffix means the boundary is after the domain
The candidates are 0 through n - 1. If all are false, each false result moves the lower boundary past the tested candidate until left and right converge at the exclusive endpoint n.

items: n is a boundary in the result domain [0, n], not a candidate to evaluate.
Returning n distinguishes all-false from a true candidate at n - 1.
Callers must interpret n as no true candidate and must not evaluate or dereference it as an in-domain value.

blocks.title: Sentinel contract
blocks.text: A first-true function over [0, n) can return any boundary in [0, n]. The extra value n represents an empty true suffix.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: Because n >= 1, index 0 is a real candidate and the premise says it is false, so it cannot be returned as first true.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_minus_one: The final in-domain candidate is also false; returning it would claim a true value where none exists.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid: The final sampled candidate depends on the trace and remains false; only the converged partition boundary has the no-true sentinel meaning.

items.prompt: For n >= 2, what should a first-true search return when the predicate is true for every candidate in [0, n)?

options.text: n.

feedback.reason: The false prefix is empty and the true suffix begins at the first candidate.

blocks.text: The transition is at the left endpoint
With n >= 1 and every candidate true, the earliest candidate 0 already satisfies P. A first-true search must retain true midpoints and keep narrowing toward earlier candidates until it reaches 0.

items: The false prefix has length zero.
The true suffix is the entire domain [0, n).
Its first index is 0, so neither n - 1 nor n satisfies the leftmost-result contract.

blocks.title: Endpoint regression test
blocks.text: All-true catches an update that discards a true midpoint or stops at any true value instead of continuing to the first one.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_minus_one: That is the last candidate, not the first true.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n: The sentinel n represents an empty true suffix, but the premise gives a true candidate immediately at index 0.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.minus_one: The canonical first-true boundary is in [0, n], and all-true places it at the legal first candidate 0 rather than outside the domain.

items.prompt: Why must the candidate domain itself be ordered for predicate binary search?

options.text: Only numeric values can be ordered.
The predicate values are sorted automatically.
The notions of candidates before and after mid must correspond to the monotonic implication.
A midpoint can exist only in an array.

feedback.reason: Monotonicity relates predicate truth to candidate order.

blocks.text: Binary search needs a meaningful before and after

A monotonic implication compares candidates: for a <= b, truth or falsity at one constrains the other. Midpoint evaluation is useful only if all candidates on one ordered side can be described by that implication.

items: Integers, dates, versions, strings under a comparator, and custom ranks can all supply an order.
The domain also needs a way to select a middle candidate and make measurable progress.
Ordering candidates does not automatically sort predicate truth; monotonicity remains a separate semantic proof.

blocks.title: Non-array domains are valid
blocks.text: The candidate range may be implicit. An integer threshold search computes a middle value without storing candidates in an array.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_numeric_only: Strings, versions, dates, and custom domains can also be ordered.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_predicate: Monotonicity must be proven, not produced by the search.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_requires_array: Integer and other indexable value domains can be searched without an array.

items.prompt: A predicate depends on mutable global state and can return different values for the same candidate during one search. What is the defect?

options.text: The result remains correct but may be slower.
The midpoint necessarily overflows.
The candidate domain now contains duplicate indices.
The search no longer has a stable monotonic partition to preserve.

feedback.reason: Binary search assumes predicate evaluations describe one fixed ordered partition.

blocks.text: Earlier eliminations rely on permanent truth

After P(mid) classifies one side as impossible, ordinary binary search never checks that region again. If mutable external state can change P(mid), the proof used to discard that side may no longer describe the same problem.

items: At time 1, P(5) = false may move left past 5.
If global state changes and P(5) later becomes true, candidate 5 may be the boundary but has already been discarded.
Freeze the relevant snapshot or make state an explicit fixed input to restore one stable partition.

blocks.title: Determinism is not only performance
blocks.text: Caching or reevaluating an unstable predicate may change which answer is returned. This is a correctness failure, not merely extra work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_slower: If truth changes after a branch, an earlier elimination can remove the candidate that is now the boundary, producing a wrong result rather than merely extra work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_overflow: The stated defect occurs even with exact midpoint arithmetic because the same candidate no longer has one stable classification.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates: Candidate identities and indices have not duplicated; mutable state has changed the semantic truth value attached to an existing candidate.

items.prompt: Which statement proves that predicate P is false-to-true monotonic?

options.text: P was true for one large test value.
For any a <= b, P(a) = true implies P(b) = true.
The input data used by P is sorted.
The first midpoint tested was true.

feedback.reason: The implication prevents truth from reverting to false as candidates increase.

blocks.text: Quantify over every ordered pair
False-to-true monotonicity is a global statement: for any candidates a <= b, P(a) = true implies P(b) = true. Once truth appears, it persists at every later candidate.

items: The contrapositive is: if P(b) is false, then P(a) is false for every a <= b.
That contrapositive justifies discarding mid and all earlier candidates after a false midpoint.
One true example or one true midpoint does not constrain every ordered pair and therefore is not a proof.

blocks.title: How to prove it in a problem
blocks.text: Start with an arbitrary witness that makes candidate a true, then show the same witness or a relaxed constraint makes every b >= a true.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_example: One large true value shows existence but does not prove that truth persists for all still larger values or locate the transition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_inputs: Sorted input can support a monotonic predicate, but an arbitrary computation over sorted values can still alternate or depend on unrelated state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_true: A true first midpoint is one observation; monotonicity must hold for every ordered pair, including candidates the search never samples.

items.prompt: Which truth sequences are monotonic with at most one transition? Select all that apply.

options.text: false, false, false.
true, false, true.
false, false, true, true.
true, true, true.

feedback.reason: A monotonic boundary may occur at an endpoint or outside the concrete candidates.

blocks.text: Count truth reversals, including zero
A false-to-true sequence allows zero or one transition. All false means the transition lies after the concrete domain; all true means it lies at or before the first candidate.

items: false, false, false: zero transitions and an empty true suffix.
true, true, true: zero transitions and an empty false prefix.
false, false, true, true: exactly one permitted transition.
true, false, true: two reversals, so truth is not persistent in either direction.

blocks.title: Constants are monotonic
blocks.text: A monotonic predicate need not contain both truth values. Sentinel behavior gives all-false and all-true domains precise boundary results.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.true_false_true: Truth becomes false and then true again, producing two transitions and invalidating whole-side elimination.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_false: Zero transitions are allowed; the first-true boundary is the upper sentinel after the domain.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_true: Zero transitions are allowed; the first true boundary is the first candidate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.false_true: Truth changes exactly once from false to true and then persists.

items.prompt: Which predicates are monotonic in the stated increasing candidate direction? Select all that apply.

options.text: A capacity x is sufficient, when larger capacity cannot make the schedule infeasible.
x is even.
In an ascending array, the value at index i is at least target.
x equals one fixed target over all integers.

feedback.reason: Monotonic predicates preserve truth or falsity in one direction.

blocks.text: Test persistence as the candidate increases
For each option, ask whether becoming true can later become false again in the stated increasing direction.

items: Capacity sufficient: a schedule that works at x still works with more capacity, so truth persists.
sorted[i] >= target: ascending order ensures every later index also has a value >= target.
x is even: truth alternates at each integer.
x equals target: truth is false before target, true at target, and false after it.

blocks.title: Equality versus threshold
blocks.text: Exact equality usually creates an isolated true point. Rephrasing it as >= or > can create a boundary predicate when the underlying domain is ordered.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.parity: Even and odd integers alternate, so a true midpoint does not imply that later candidates remain true.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.exact_value: Exact equality creates a single true point surrounded by false values, which has two transitions rather than one persistent region.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.capacity: Reusing any feasible schedule at a larger capacity proves false-to-true persistence.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_threshold: Ascending order proves that once sorted[i] >= target, every later value also satisfies the predicate.

items.prompt: Which steps are required before binary-searching a custom predicate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Define an ordered finite or convergent candidate domain.
Assume monotonicity because the code computes mid.
Prove the truth implication across the candidate order.
Define exactly what true and false mean.

feedback.reason: Predicate search is a modeling exercise before it is a loop template.

blocks.text: Three modeling obligations justify elimination
A midpoint expression is only mechanics. Correctness requires a searchable order, an exact meaning for one boolean result, and a proof connecting that result to every candidate on one side.

items: Ordered domain: defines before, after, boundaries, and a progress-making midpoint or split.
Predicate semantics: states every constraint covered by true and false for one candidate.
Monotonicity proof: establishes the implication used to remove a whole side.
Only after these facts can first-true, last-true, or a complementary boundary be selected.

blocks.title: Syntax is not evidence
blocks.text: Computing mid proves neither that candidates are meaningfully ordered nor that P(mid) classifies either side.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.assume_mid: A midpoint merely samples the domain; monotonicity must come from the problem's semantics and an implication across candidate order.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.ordered_domain: The search needs meaningful sides, enclosing endpoints, and a way to split candidates while progressing.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.predicate_semantics: Branch correctness depends on exactly what true and false guarantee about one candidate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.prove_monotonicity: The cross-candidate implication is what justifies eliminating an entire half after one evaluation.

items.prompt: Which edge cases should a first-true predicate search handle? Select all that apply.

options.text: The predicate is true for the whole domain.
The predicate alternates true and false.
The transition is at the first or last candidate.
The predicate is false for the whole domain.

feedback.reason: Endpoint and absent transitions are legitimate monotonic cases.

blocks.text: Test all legal locations of the first-true boundary
For candidates [0, n), the first-true boundary can be 0, any internal candidate, or the sentinel n. Tests must exercise both extremes and transitions beside an endpoint.

items: All true returns 0 and checks left-endpoint retention.
All false returns n or the documented not-found result and checks sentinel handling.
Transition at the first or last candidate checks off-by-one updates.
A two-candidate domain checks that both branches strictly progress.

blocks.title: Alternation is not an edge case
blocks.text: A true/false alternation violates the monotonicity precondition itself. Expected behavior is to reject the model or use another algorithm, not to make boundary search handle it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.alternating_required: Alternation has multiple transitions and therefore falls outside the first-true contract instead of testing a legal boundary position.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_true: The false prefix is empty, so the correct first-true result is the first candidate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_false: The true suffix is empty, so the result must be the upper sentinel or the contract's explicit not-found state.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.transition_edges: These cases expose whether updates preserve and eventually evaluate the first or last concrete candidate.

items.prompt: Arrange the design process for monotonic predicate search.

elements.text: Define the feasibility or validity predicate.
Prove the predicate has one directional transition.
Select first true, last true, first false, or last false and implement matching updates.

feedback.reason: The search template follows from the direction and desired side of the transition.

blocks.text: Derive the template instead of selecting it first

Every later step depends on the preceding model. Candidate order defines sides; predicate meaning makes one evaluation trustworthy; the transition proof determines which side is impossible; only then can updates be chosen.
Dependency order

items: Define the ordered finite domain or a convergent domain with an explicit stopping rule.
Define exactly what P(x) means for one candidate, including every constraint and fixed input snapshot.
Prove false-to-true or true-to-false persistence across that order.
Choose the requested transition side and derive an interval, midpoint bias, updates, sentinel, and postcondition that preserve it.

blocks.title: Stop if the proof fails
blocks.text: A familiar loop is not a fallback for a nonmonotonic model. Reformulate the candidate or predicate, or choose another algorithm.

items.prompt: Which mechanics belong to a first-true search over a false-to-true predicate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Choose mid inside the active candidate interval.
Return mid immediately whenever P(mid) is true.
If true, retain mid and search the left side.
If false, discard mid and every smaller candidate.

feedback.reason: Truth means the first true is at or before mid; falsity means it is strictly after mid.

blocks.text: Both branches preserve the same boundary
Let b be the first true candidate. A midpoint must lie inside the active domain; then the false-to-true implication determines which candidates can be removed.

items: P(mid) = true proves b <= mid. Retain mid and search the left side because mid may equal b.
P(mid) = false proves b > mid. Discard mid and every smaller candidate.
The exact assignments—such as right = mid and left = mid + 1—must match the chosen interval convention.
Immediate return on a true midpoint proves validity but not that an earlier true candidate is absent.

blocks.title: Branch proof template
blocks.text: State where b lies relative to mid, then state why the updated interval still contains b and has become smaller.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_true_mid: A true midpoint may lie inside the true suffix after its first element, so immediate return can violate the leftmost result contract.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.compute_mid: An in-range midpoint is required before the predicate can classify either ordered side safely.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.true_keep_left: Truth places the first true boundary at or before mid, and mid itself must remain possible.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.false_discard_left: Falsity plus monotonicity places the first true boundary strictly after mid, eliminating the whole left region.

items.prompt: A monotonic predicate over W integer candidates costs O(1) per evaluation. Select search time and iterative auxiliary space.
constraints: Each iteration reduces the candidate interval by about half.

feedback.reason: The logarithm depends on candidate-domain width rather than necessarily on input length.

blocks.text: Halve W candidates
After k iterations, repeated halving leaves at most about W / 2^k candidates. Reaching one candidate requires k = O(log W), and each evaluation costs O(1).
Time and space

items: Predicate evaluations: O(log W).
Time per evaluation: O(1), so total time is O(log W).
The iterative search retains only boundaries, midpoint, and a constant number of boolean values.
Auxiliary space is therefore O(1).

blocks.title: W is the searched width
blocks.text: If the candidate range is numeric and much wider than the input, log W—not necessarily log n—controls the number of evaluations.

items.prompt: A monotonic predicate scans n input elements in O(n) time, and the integer candidate range contains W values. Select total search time and outer-search auxiliary space.
constraints: The predicate is evaluated independently at each binary-search iteration.
Predicate-local temporary memory is excluded from the requested outer-search space.

feedback.reason: Binary search limits predicate calls, but each call still scans n values.

blocks.text: Multiply predicate cost by candidate levels
The outer search performs O(log W) iterations for W >= 2 candidates. The prompt says each independent predicate evaluation scans n elements, so one iteration costs O(n).
Time and outer space

items: Evaluations: O(log W).
Work per evaluation: O(n).
Total time: O(n) × O(log W) = O(n log W).
The iterative outer loop itself stores only constant scalar state, so its requested auxiliary space is O(1).

blocks.title: Space scope is explicit
blocks.text: Whole-algorithm space would add predicate-local temporary memory. This question intentionally asks only for the outer search's own storage.
